claim: Adult vertebrate nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) are allosteric proteins that mediate synaptic transmission between motor neurons and skeletal muscle fibers.
source: Adult vertebrate nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) are allosteric proteins that mediate synaptic transmission between motor neurons and skeletal muscle fibers.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about AChR function, supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: Adult vertebrate nicotinic AChRs are pentameric ligand-gated ion channels composed of four different subunits (2 α1, β1, δ, ε) arranged symmetrically around a central ion-conducting pore.
source: These pentameric ligand-gated ion channels are composed of four different subunits (2 α1, β1, δ, ε) arranged symmetrically around a central ion-conducting pore (Rahman et al., 2020; Unwin, 1993).
evidence: This structural description is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Interactions between acetylcholine and orthosteric sites in the extracellular domain increase the probability of a global conformational change that opens a gate in the transmembrane domain approximately 60 Å away.
source: Interactions between the neurotransmitter acetylcholine (ACh) and orthosteric sites in the extracellular domain (ECD) increase the probability of a global change in protein conformation that opens a distant (~60 Å) allosteric site (a 'gate') in the transmembrane domain (TMD), allowing cations to cross the membrane.
evidence: This describes the allosteric mechanism of AChR activation, supported by established knowledge.

claim: In AChRs, ligand-protein interactions occur sequentially in reactions called 'touch' (initial contact), 'catch' (agonist recognition), and 'hold' (receptor animation).
source: In AChRs the ligand-protein interactions occur sequentially in reactions called 'touch' (initial contact), 'catch' (agonist recognition), and 'hold' (receptor animation) (Auerbach, 2024; Jadey and Auerbach, 2012).
evidence: This sequential mechanism is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The neurotransmitter sites switch from low- to high-affinity (L→H) at the start of the global gating isomerization.
source: The neurotransmitter sites switch from low- to high-affinity (L→H) at the start of the global gating isomerization, and the gate switches from closed to open at the end of the isomerization (C→O) (Grosman et al., 2000; Purohit et al., 2013b).
evidence: This temporal sequence is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The gate switches from closed to open at the end of the gating isomerization.
source: The neurotransmitter sites switch from low- to high-affinity (L→H) at the start of the global gating isomerization, and the gate switches from closed to open at the end of the isomerization (C→O) (Grosman et al., 2000; Purohit et al., 2013b).
evidence: This temporal sequence is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: In AChRs without agonists, the probability of having the open-gate shape (PO) is approximately 10^-6.
source: In AChRs without agonists, a large energy barrier separates CLfrom OH so the probability of having the open-gate shape (PO) is small (~10–6) and the baseline current is negligible (Jackson, 1986; Nayak et al., 2012; Purohit and Auerbach, 2009).
evidence: This quantitative value is supported by citations to experimental measurements.

claim: The higher affinity of OH compared to CL indicates that agonists provide extra binding energy to stabilize the open state preferentially, increasing PO and membrane current.
source: The higher affinity of OH compared to CL indicates that agonists provide extra binding energy to stabilize this state preferentially, increasing PO and membrane current.
evidence: This is an inference from the differential affinity states and their functional consequences.

claim: Agonists stabilize the gating transition state to nearly the same extent as the end state.
source: Importantly, agonists also stabilize the gating transition state (the separating barrier) to nearly the same extent as the end state, so the agonist-induced increase in PO is caused almost exclusively by an increase in the channel-opening rate constant.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference about transition state stabilization.

claim: The agonist-induced increase in PO is caused almost exclusively by an increase in the channel-opening rate constant.
source: Importantly, agonists also stabilize the gating transition state (the separating barrier) to nearly the same extent as the end state, so the agonist-induced increase in PO is caused almost exclusively by an increase in the channel-opening rate constant.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion based on transition state theory and experimental observations.

claim: Each orthosteric site in adult AChRs has two affinities: weak to L and strong to H.
source: Each orthosteric site has two affinities (agonist binding free energies), weak to L and strong to H.
evidence: This is a fundamental property of the allosteric model for AChRs.

claim: The difference in binding free energies (ΔGH-ΔGL) is the energy source that drives the otherwise unfavorable protein isomerization.
source: Their difference, H minus L (ΔGH-ΔGL), is the energy source that drives the otherwise unfavorable protein isomerization.
evidence: This is a thermodynamic principle applied to the allosteric mechanism.

claim: Agonist efficiency depends on the H/L binding free energy ratio, (1-ΔGL/ΔGH).
source: A related, but distinct, agonist property is efficiency that, in contrast to efficacy, depends on the H/L binding free energy ratio, (1-ΔGL/ΔGH) (Nayak et al., 2019).
evidence: This definition of efficiency is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Efficiency determines the fraction of binding free energy converted into local movements that stabilize the gating transition state.
source: This ratio determines the fraction of binding free energy converted into local movements that stabilize the gating transition state and, hence, animate the protein.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the efficiency parameter.

claim: Adult-type muscle AChRs have two approximately equal and independent neurotransmitter sites.
source: These receptors have two approximately equal and independent neurotransmitter sites (Nayak and Auerbach, 2017).
evidence: This structural and functional property is supported by a citation.

claim: The total free energy change in the L→H transition for two neurotransmitters is –10.2 kcal/mol.
source: The total free energy change in the L→H transition for two neurotransmitters (–10.2 kcal/mol), added to the unfavorable unliganded isomerization free energy change (+8.3 kcal/mol at –100 mV), generates a favorable free energy change of gating (–1.9 kcal/mol) (Nayak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental measurement cited from previous work.

claim: The unfavorable unliganded isomerization free energy change is +8.3 kcal/mol at –100 mV.
source: The total free energy change in the L→H transition for two neurotransmitters (–10.2 kcal/mol), added to the unfavorable unliganded isomerization free energy change (+8.3 kcal/mol at –100 mV), generates a favorable free energy change of gating (–1.9 kcal/mol) (Nayak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental measurement cited from previous work.

claim: The two independent L→H rearrangements increase the gating equilibrium constant by a factor of 56802.
source: Accordingly, the two independent L→H rearrangements add to increase the gating equilibrium constant by a factor of 56802, to increase PO from 7.4 × ~10–7 to 0.96 (Nayak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a quantitative calculation based on experimental data cited from previous work.

claim: The L→H rearrangements increase the opening rate constant from approximately 0.001 s^-1 to approximately 50,000 s^-1.
source: Likewise, the L→H rearrangements increase the opening rate constant by almost the same factor, from ~0.001 s–1 to ~50,000 s–1.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of rate constants based on experimental observations.

claim: MD simulations reveal that the L→H transition involves the agonist pivoting around its cationic center ('flip').
source: Using four agonists spanning three η-classes, the simulations reveal the structural basis of the L→H transition where: the agonist pivots around its cationic center ('flip'), loop C undergoes staged downward displacement ('flop'), and a compact, stable high-affinity pocket forms ('fix').
evidence: This is a primary finding from the MD simulations reported in this study.

claim: MD simulations reveal that the L→H transition involves loop C undergoing staged downward displacement ('flop').
source: Using four agonists spanning three η-classes, the simulations reveal the structural basis of the L→H transition where: the agonist pivots around its cationic center ('flip'), loop C undergoes staged downward displacement ('flop'), and a compact, stable high-affinity pocket forms ('fix').
evidence: This is a primary finding from the MD simulations reported in this study.

claim: MD simulations reveal that the L→H transition involves formation of a compact, stable high-affinity pocket ('fix').
source: Using four agonists spanning three η-classes, the simulations reveal the structural basis of the L→H transition where: the agonist pivots around its cationic center ('flip'), loop C undergoes staged downward displacement ('flop'), and a compact, stable high-affinity pocket forms ('fix').
evidence: This is a primary finding from the MD simulations reported in this study.

claim: The efficiency (η) derived from binding energies calculated in silico matched exact values measured experimentally in vitro.
source: The η derived from binding energies calculated in silico matched exact values measured experimentally in vitro.
evidence: This is a comparison between computational and experimental results reported in this study.

claim: Intermediate states of the orthosteric site during receptor activation are apparent only in simulations.
source: Intermediate states of the orthosteric site during receptor activation are apparent only in simulations, but could potentially be observed experimentally via time-resolved structural studies.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations with speculation about future experimental validation.

claim: All four agonists docked in the cis orientation with strong binding scores ranging from –5.82 to –9.18 kcal/mol.
source: The docking simulations had strong binding scores ranging from –5.82 to –9.18 kcal/mol (Figure 2A), suggesting that the interactions were stable.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from docking simulations shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The docked agonist's tail pointed towards (cis) rather than away (trans) from the α subunit, unlike the orientation in cryo-EM structures of desensitized receptors.
source: However, unlike the agonist orientation apparent in cryo-EM structures of DH (Noviello et al., 2021; Rahman et al., 2022; Rahman et al., 2020; Walsh et al., 2018; Zarkadas et al., 2022; Figure 1D), the docked agonist's tail pointed towards (cis) rather than away (trans) from the α subunit (Figure 2B, top).
evidence: This is a comparison between docking results and cryo-EM structures, with references to figures.

claim: The cis orientation was a consistent result for the three top docking poses for all four ligands.
source: This was a consistent result that pertained to the three top docking poses for all four ligands.
evidence: This describes the consistency of the docking results across multiple poses and ligands.

claim: All 200 top docking scores for CCh showed cis orientation with the tail pointing towards the α subunit.
source: We examined the top 200 docking scores for CCh. All poses were cis, with the tail pointing towards the α subunit and away from the main cluster of aromatic side chains.
evidence: This is an extended analysis of docking results for CCh.

claim: All 200 ns MD simulations for all three replicates for all four agonists showed similar RMSD patterns with differences consistently below 1 Å.
source: The 200 ns simulations for all three replicates for all four agonists showed similar root-mean-square-deviation (RMSD) patterns with differences consistently below 1 Å (Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1) suggesting that the trajectories were sufficiently robust and reproducible.
evidence: This is a quantitative assessment of simulation reproducibility shown in Figure 2C.

claim: All systems became stable by approximately 120 ns in the MD simulations.
source: Although there were initial deviations, all systems became stable by ~120 ns.
evidence: This is an observation about simulation convergence.

claim: The RMSF of the Cα atoms showed flexibility around the pocket mainly in loops C and F (but not E).
source: The root-mean-square-fluctuation (RMSF) of the Cα atoms showed flexibility around the pocket mainly in loops C and F (but not E) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a structural analysis result from the simulations shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Agonists stabilize binding pocket residues compared to apo simulations.
source: In addition, RMSD measurements show that, while agonists stabilize binding pocket residues (compared to apo; Figure 2—figure supplement 2), interfacial residues continue to fluctuate in the presence of agonists.
evidence: This is a comparison between agonist-bound and apo simulations shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Interfacial residues continue to fluctuate in the presence of agonists.
source: In addition, RMSD measurements show that, while agonists stabilize binding pocket residues (compared to apo; Figure 2—figure supplement 2), interfacial residues continue to fluctuate in the presence of agonists.
evidence: This is an observation from RMSD analysis shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: There is no experimental evidence that the ECD-TMD interfacial region influences agonist binding energy.
source: However, there is no experimental evidence that the ECD-TMD interfacial region influences agonist binding energy, and (as described below) the match between experimental binding energies (whole receptors) and those calculated in the simulations (ECD dimers) further discounts this proposal.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of experimental evidence, supported by inference from the simulation results.

claim: The interfacial region plays an important role in setting the unliganded gating equilibrium constant (L0) but not agonist affinity (KL or KH).
source: The interfacial region plays an important role in setting the unliganded gating equilibrium constant (L0) but not agonist affinity (KL or KH)
evidence: This is a functional distinction based on experimental knowledge.

claim: For all ligands and in all trajectories, the ligand orientation inverted from cis to trans during the simulations.
source: For all ligands and in all trajectories, at the start of the simulations, the agonist's tail points towards the α subunit and at the end, it points towards δ. This re-orientation represents a nearly complete somersault (a 'flip') about the agonist's main cationic center (N+) that remains surrounded by the αW149-αY190-αY198 aromatic side chain cluster throughout (see Figure 5; Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is a consistent observation across all simulations, with reference to figures.

claim: The agonist's cationic center (N+) remains surrounded by the αW149-αY190-αY198 aromatic side chain cluster throughout the flip.
source: This re-orientation represents a nearly complete somersault (a 'flip') about the agonist's main cationic center (N+) that remains surrounded by the αW149-αY190-αY198 aromatic side chain cluster throughout (see Figure 5; Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the simulations shown in figures.

claim: The final MD configuration with CCh aligns well with the CCh-bound cryo-EM desensitized structure (7QL6; RMSD <0.5 Å).
source: The final MD configuration (with CCh) aligns well with the CCh-bound cryo-EM desensitized structure (7QL6; RMSD <0.5 Å) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between simulation and experimental structure shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: The final trans orientation with CCh remains constant for at least 1 μs.
source: Video 2 shows that the final, trans orientation with CCh remains constant for at least 1 μs, indicating that the structure had settled by 200 ns with no further major rearrangements.
evidence: This is an observation from extended simulation shown in Video 2.

claim: In experiments, ACH and ADH have the same CCh binding free energy.
source: This result is consistent with functional measurements showing that D and O AChRs have indistinguishable affinities (citations in Auerbach, 2020).
evidence: This is an experimental observation cited from previous work.

claim: Local rearrangements in an ECD pentamer docked with ACh were similar to those in the dimer, including the cis→trans flip of agonist.
source: First, the local rearrangements were similar in an ECD pentamer docked with ACh to those in the dimer, including the cis→trans flip of agonist (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a comparison between pentamer and dimer simulations shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: 200 ns simulations of the apo ECD dimer show similar RMSF and RMSD patterns to those with ligand present (CCh).
source: Second, 200 ns simulations of the apo ECD dimer show similar RMSF and RMSD patterns to those with ligand present (CCh) (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A and B).
evidence: This is a comparison between apo and ligand-bound simulations shown in supplementary figures.

claim: In apo simulations, loop C flops partially to narrow the aqueous connection between the bath and the pocket.
source: Third, in these simulations the downward displacement of loop C apparent with agonists (see below) was present, but less pronounced (Figure 2—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: This is an observation from apo simulations shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: After removing CCh from the final 200 ns MD structure and re-docking all four agonists, the preferred poses for all were trans.
source: To test whether rearrangements in the simulations served to enforce the trans pose, we removed the bound CCh from the final 200 ns MD structure and re-docked all four agonists. The preferred poses for all were trans (Figure 2A, bottom).
evidence: This is a result from re-docking experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Binding energies from docking scores were higher for the final 200 ns structures compared to initial structures, consistent with an L-to-H transition.
source: In addition, binding energies from docking scores were higher for the final 200 ns structures, consistent with an L-to-H transition (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a comparison of docking scores shown in Figure 2B.

claim: For all four agonists, all trajectories started in m1 and ended in m3, with m2 occurring as an intermediate.
source: For all four agonists, all trajectories started in m1 and ended in m3, with m2 occurring as an intermediate (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a temporal sequence observed in the simulations shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: For all agonists, the m3 pose was more localized and stable compared to m1, with m2 being the least stable pose.
source: For all agonists, the m3 pose was more localized and stable compared to m1, with m2 being the least stable pose.
evidence: This is a comparative analysis of the stability of different states from the simulations.

claim: The m2 basin in the PCA plots for ACh was especially broad and shallow.
source: The only exception was m2 for ACh which was shallow, indicating a less stable intermediate state between m1 and m3.
evidence: This is an observation from PCA analysis specific to ACh.

claim: BPMD calculations consistently showed lower scores for m3 compared to m1, indicating higher ligand stability.
source: The BPMD calculations, which use CompositeScores derived from PoseScore (measuring ligand stability based on RMSD) and PersScore (evaluating the persistence of key ligand-protein interactions), were performed to assess stability. The BPMD scores consistently showed lower scores for m3 compared to m1, indicating higher ligand stability (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a result from BPMD calculations shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: The trans orientation in m3 was more stable than cis in m1 for all four ligands.
source: Furthermore, the trans orientation in m3 was more stable than cis in m1, for all four ligands.
evidence: This is a comparative stability assessment from BPMD calculations.

claim: For ACh and CCh, there was excellent agreement between ΔGm1 and ΔGL and between ΔGm3 and ΔGH.
source: For ACh and CCh, there was excellent agreement between ΔGm1 and ΔGL and between ΔGm3 and ΔGH.
evidence: This is a comparison between calculated and experimental binding energies.

claim: For Ebt and Ebx, the calculated binding energy values overestimated experimental ones by approximately 45% (Ebt) and approximately 130% (Ebx).
source: The match was worse for the other 2 agonists, with the calculated values overestimating experimental ones by ~45% (Ebt) and ~130% (Ebx).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between calculated and experimental values.

claim: In all cases, ΔGm3 was more favorable than ΔGm1.
source: However, in all cases, ΔGm3 was more favorable than ΔGm1, and the % overestimation compared to experimental values was approximately the same for m1 versus m3.
evidence: This is a consistent trend observed across all agonists in the calculations.

claim: Efficiency values calculated in silico agreed almost perfectly with those measured experimentally.
source: Figure 4A right (Figure 4—source data 1) shows that efficiency values calculated in silico agreed almost perfectly with those measured experimentally.
evidence: This is a comparison between calculated and experimental efficiency values shown in Figure 4A.

claim: All agonists showed an increase in Van der Waals (VdW) interaction energy in the hold rearrangement.
source: All agonists showed an increase in Van der Waals (VdW) interaction energy in the hold rearrangement.
evidence: This is a consistent observation across all agonists from energy calculations.

claim: The calculated (PBSA) increase in VdW interactions was most pronounced with Ebt and least for Ebx, with CCh and ACh falling in between.
source: The calculated (PBSA) increase was most pronounced with Ebt and least for Ebx, with CCh and ACh falling in between (Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is a comparative analysis of VdW interactions shown in source data.

claim: There is a reduction in binding pocket volume in the L→H transition.
source: A compaction of the pocket is also apparent in Figure 4C that shows a reduction in binding pocket volume, and in Figure 4D that shows a decrease in the number of water molecules.
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There is a decrease in the number of water molecules in the pocket in the L→H transition.
source: A compaction of the pocket is also apparent in Figure 4C that shows a reduction in binding pocket volume, and in Figure 4D that shows a decrease in the number of water molecules.
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 4D.

claim: On average, the ligands underwent a >130° pivot about the N+-αW149 fulcrum.
source: On average, the ligands underwent a >130o pivot about the N+-αW149 fulcrum (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of the agonist rotation shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The flip of the agonist began at the start of the simulation (m1).
source: Also, in all instances, the flip began at the start of the simulation (m1).
evidence: This is a temporal observation about when the flip initiates.

claim: Loop C flop was measured as the displacement of its tip (Cα of αC192) in m3 relative to its apo position.
source: In the simulations, loop C flop was measured as the displacement of its tip (Cα of αC192) in m3 relative to its apo position.
evidence: This describes the method used to quantify loop C displacement.

claim: The distance traveled by loop C varied with the agonist.
source: The distance traveled varied with the agonist (Figure 6—source data 1) but we do not discern a pattern in the extent of loop C flop with regard to agonist affinity, efficacy or efficiency.
evidence: This is an observation about variability in loop C displacement shown in source data.

claim: In L, αY190, αY93, and δW57 are spaced apart, providing an open slot that accommodates the agonist's tail in the cis orientation.
source: In L, αY190, αY93, and δW57 are spaced apart, providing an open slot that accommodates the agonist's tail in the cis orientation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the simulations shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: In H, loop C flop repositions αY190 closer to αY93, effectively filling the gap to create a unified surface.
source: However, in H, loop C flop repositions αY190 closer to αY93, effectively filling the gap to create a unified surface.
evidence: This is a structural observation about the H state from the simulations.

claim: With ACh, deleting the aromatic ring at position 149 (A versus W) results in a loss of 3.0 kcal/mol for ΔGL and 5.3 kcal/mol for ΔGH.
source: With ACh, deleting the ring (A versus W at 149, A versus F for 190 and 198) results in a loss (kcal/mol) of 3.0, 0.9, 2.1 for ΔGL and 5.3, 2.8, 4.0 for ΔGH, respectively (Purohit et al., 2014).
evidence: This is experimental data from mutagenesis studies cited from previous work.

claim: With ACh, deleting the aromatic ring at position 190 (A versus F) results in a loss of 0.9 kcal/mol for ΔGL and 2.8 kcal/mol for ΔGH.
source: With ACh, deleting the ring (A versus W at 149, A versus F for 190 and 198) results in a loss (kcal/mol) of 3.0, 0.9, 2.1 for ΔGL and 5.3, 2.8, 4.0 for ΔGH, respectively (Purohit et al., 2014).
evidence: This is experimental data from mutagenesis studies cited from previous work.

claim: With ACh, deleting the aromatic ring at position 198 (A versus F) results in a loss of 2.1 kcal/mol for ΔGL and 4.0 kcal/mol for ΔGH.
source: With ACh, deleting the ring (A versus W at 149, A versus F for 190 and 198) results in a loss (kcal/mol) of 3.0, 0.9, 2.1 for ΔGL and 5.3, 2.8, 4.0 for ΔGH, respectively (Purohit et al., 2014).
evidence: This is experimental data from mutagenesis studies cited from previous work.

claim: αW149 is the main player in both L and H binding, but the biggest binding energy increase in hold comes from αY190.
source: αW149 (in loop B) is the main player in both L and H, but the biggest binding energy increase in hold comes from αY190 (in loop C).
evidence: This is an inference from the mutagenesis data about the relative contributions of residues.

claim: In the simulations, the distance between the main aromatic groups and N+ decreases only slightly in the L→H transition.
source: In the simulations, the distance between these main aromatic groups and N+ decreases only slightly, L→H (Figure 6, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the simulations shown in Figure 6.

claim: The aromatic cluster appears to act as a slippery anchor (a ball joint) that maintains the stability of the N+ position even as the tail rotates within it.
source: This aromatic cluster appears to act as a slippery anchor (a ball joint) that maintains the stability of the N+ position even as the tail rotates within it, approximately doubling agonist binding energy.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the structural observations from the simulations.

claim: In m1, a functional group in the agonist tail interacts with αY93 for all agonists.
source: In m1, a functional group in the agonist tail interacts with αY93 (all agonists) and αD200 (only CCh, and Ebt).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the simulations about interactions in the m1 state.

claim: In m1, a functional group in the agonist tail interacts with αD200 for CCh and Ebt only.
source: In m1, a functional group in the agonist tail interacts with αY93 (all agonists) and αD200 (only CCh, and Ebt).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the simulations about interactions in the m1 state.

claim: The position and orientation of αW149 relative to N+ of the agonist remains nearly unchanged m1→m2→m3 and serves as a fulcrum for the cis→trans flip.
source: The position and orientation of αW149 relative to N+ of the agonist remains nearly unchanged m1→m2→m3 and serves as a fulcrum for the cis→trans flip (see Figure 5).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: In m2, the functional nitrogen at the agonist tail (CCh, Ebt, and Ebx) interacts with the hydroxyl group of αY198.
source: In m2, the functional nitrogen at the agonist tail (CCh, Ebt, and Ebx) interacts with the hydroxyl group of αY198.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the simulations about interactions in the m2 state.

claim: For all ligands, αY190 repositioning and loop C flop (m1→m3) are correlated.
source: For all ligands, αY190 repositioning and loop C flop (m1→m3) are correlated.
evidence: This is a correlation observed across all ligands in the simulations.

claim: In m3, the agonist fully flips to trans, facilitating VdW interactions, de-wetting, and the formation of water-mediated hydrogen bonds with the reactive group at its tail with δN109/δL121 backbone via a structural water.
source: In m3, the agonist fully flips to trans, facilitating VdW interactions, de-wetting, and the formation of water-mediated hydrogen bonds with the reactive group at its tail with δN109/δL121 backbone (loop E) via a structural water.
evidence: This is a comprehensive structural description of the m3 state from the simulations.

claim: The agonist's flip starts the m1→m2 transition.
source: The agonist's flip starts the m1→m2 transition, and the establishment of this water-mediated H-bond is completed in m2→m3 (Figure 6; Video 2).
evidence: This is a temporal sequence observed in the simulations shown in Figure 6 and Video 2.

claim: The establishment of the water-mediated H-bond is completed in m2→m3.
source: The agonist's flip starts the m1→m2 transition, and the establishment of this water-mediated H-bond is completed in m2→m3 (Figure 6; Video 2).
evidence: This is a temporal sequence observed in the simulations shown in Figure 6 and Video 2.

claim: The mutation αK145A lowers the efficiencies of ACh and CCh (from 0.51 to 0.41) but has no effect on those of Ebt and Ebx (that remain at 0.41 and 0.46).
source: Interestingly, the mutation αK145A lowers the efficiencies of ACh and CCh (from 0.51 to 0.41) but has no effect on those of Ebt and Ebx (that remain at 0.41 and 0.46) (Indurthi and Auerbach, 2023).

claim: In the hold simulations, the αK145-αD200 distance increases from 4.4 Å in apo to 6.1 or 5.1 Å in ACL (CCh or ACh).
source: In the hold simulations, the αK145-αD200 distance (Å) increases from only 4.4 in apo to 6.1 or 5.1 in ACL (CCh or ACh).

claim: In ACL→ACH, with ACh and CCh the αK145-αD200 separation shortens substantially to 2.8 or 2.6 Å, making it more rigid.
source: In ACL→ACH, with ACh and CCh the αK145-αD200 separation (Å) shortens substantially to 2.8 or 2.6, making it more rigid.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the simulations.

claim: With Ebt and Ebx the αK145-αD200 distance remains unstable, fluctuating between 3–6 Å throughout the course of the simulation.
source: However, with Ebt and Ebx the αK145-αD200 distance remains unstable, fluctuating between 3–6 Å throughout the course of the simulation.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the simulations showing agonist-dependent behavior.

claim: The αK145-αY190 distance stabilizes at 5.3 Å or 6.1 Å in ACH with ACh and CCh but continues to fluctuate with Ebt and Ebx.
source: Likewise, αK145-αY190 distance stabilizes at 5.3 Å or 6.1 Å in ACH with ACh and CCh but continues to fluctuate with Ebt and Ebx.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the simulations showing agonist-dependent behavior.

claim: The αY190-αD200 distance remains stable in ACH for all ligands.
source: In contrast, the αY190-αD200 distance remains stable in ACH for all ligands.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the simulations showing consistency across ligands.

claim: The instability in the αK145-αD200 and αK145-αY190 distances can primarily be attributed to αK145.
source: This suggests that the instability in the αK145-αD200 and αK145-αY190 distances can primarily be attributed to αK145 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference from the distance measurements shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Agreements between cryo-EM (apo and desensitized) versus simulated (apo and CH) structures support the proposal that the simulated m1 and m3 structures reflect ACL and ACH.
source: Nonetheless, agreements between cryo-EM (apo and desensitized) versus simulated (apo and CH) structures, and between ΔGL and ΔGH free energies estimated from electrophysiology versus simulations, support our proposal that the simulated m1 and m3 structures reflect ACL and ACH.
